描述_ZN: The King Vajra Sutra, ink topography, cut and framed in two volumes. The upper booklet is 30 pages long and the lower booklet is 22 pages long, each half of the booklet is 26.5 cm long and about 15 cm across. The mount has 10 characters per line, and there is no seam between the lines, so it is clear that the inscription was originally divided into several layers, for the convenience of binding the volume after transmission. 　　The Vajra Sutra is an important classic of Buddhism, which was translated into six different versions in the Tang Dynasty. In the Tang Dynasty, there were six translations of the Vajra Sutra after it was introduced to China. When the Tang Emperor Wenzong Li Ang, Yang '0490', a native of Hongnong, abridged and compiled this sutra, called the "New Set of Vajra Sutra", which is known as the "Seven Translations". Yang wrote the preface and invited eight ministers, including Zheng Qin and Liu Gongquan, to inscribe the sutra praise, and put it on the stone with an eight-point book, which was installed in the Xingtang Temple in Shangdu (Chang'an). In July of the fourth year of Taihe (830), Yang Chenghe, Minister of Internal Affairs and Minister of Hongnong County, presented this "sutra" to the emperor with a certificate. In August, Emperor Wen compiled it into the "Collection of scriptures catalog", and thought that "the initial carving of the body of eight points, the reader many errors", ordered the set of Jin right general Wang Xizhi book republication, to Taihe six years (832 years) spring work completed. Li Shimin, Emperor Taizong of Tang, loved Wang Xizhi's calligraphy, so Wang became the most popular calligraphy style of the Tang generation. In the third year of Xianheng (672), Hongren, a Buddhist monk at Hongfu Temple in Chang'an, first adopted the method of "collecting characters" and carved the monument "Collecting Wang Xizhi's line script", which played a significant role in the popularization of Wang's calligraphy. Later on, his method was followed by many others. This stele is a collection of Wang by order, and is distinctive because of its excellent mold. Chen Jiru, a great calligrapher of the Ming Dynasty, even considered it more credible than the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Set King": "Wen Huang's Preface to the Holy Teachings has more than a thousand words, and Huai Ren's book on the set of the Righteous Army is not incompatible.
